# What information could resolve the ambiguity? {#sec-information}

## Motivation

If no loss can fix a continuum of exact minima, the remaining question is which *additional information* breaks the tie,
and how much of it is needed. This changes the framing from "which loss?" to "what knowledge?", and part of it can be
studied without training a network at all.

The status of the evidence matters for how this chapter should be read. Every analysis below is preliminary. The null-direction
profile was reviewed twice; the second review reproduced the numbers but again returned the finding for changes of wording,
which were made and have not been re-reviewed. The single-ray bound was also reviewed twice and the second review
supported it, but the finding was edited afterwards and is again preliminary. The spatial-field and prior analyses have not
been reviewed at all. They use a mix of validation and training cases and idealised single rays, and they are all
noise-free and around the true solution, so they are hypotheses to be tested rather than results to build on. The test that
would show whether any of this works in practice, converged per-case solves, has now had a first bounded pilot on three
validation cases (see the last section). Its findings are preliminary and, apart from an engineering note, were judged by
their one independent review to need corrections, which were made and have not been re-reviewed. The pilot supplied part of
the information (the tissue sum) from the truth, so it measures information limits and not label-free recovery.

## How visible is the null direction?

A *step of size $t$* along a direction $\mathbf{d}$ means changing the three material fractions (adipose, fibroglandular,
calcification) by $t\,\mathbf{d}$, with $\mathbf{d}$ a unit vector. Two directions matter. The *null direction* $\mathbf{n}$
is the combination of material changes that leaves the two spectral measurements unchanged to first order, computed from the
zero-thickness effective attenuation matrix. The *pure exchange* $\mathbf{s}=(-1,+1,0)/\sqrt{2}$ trades adipose for
fibroglandular tissue and leaves calcification alone.

[The exact null vector is $\mathbf{n}\approx(-0.723,\,0.691,\,-0.008)$, which is almost the pure exchange (cosine 0.9997) but not
quite: per unit step it also changes calcification by about $-0.8\%$ and the total of adipose plus fibroglandular fraction by
about $-3.1\%$, and both compensating changes are needed (compensation by calcification alone would leave about 5% of the
exchange's visibility to the data, by the total alone about 12%).]{#clm-0096 .claim}
[With this exact null vector, the root-mean-square projection error, averaged over rays, grows by about $4\times10^{-5}$ per
unit step along the null direction but about $1.3\times10^{-2}$ per unit step along the pure exchange with calcification
fixed, a ratio of about 330 (12 validation cases).]{#clm-0039 .claim} The slope along the null direction is not exactly zero
because the vector is exact only at zero path length, so first-order beam hardening leaves a small residual. A first profile
that used a three-decimal approximation of the null vector was withdrawn, because most of its apparent slope came from the
rounding; the numbers here were recomputed with the exact vector. The data in these calculations are generated by the same
forward model that is then evaluated, so a profile shows sensitivity of the loss, not robustness to model error, and whether
the truth is the unique minimiser along the null family has not been shown.

The trained networks are not simply sitting on the exact-minimum family: [the trained label-free solutions have projection
errors 4 to 6 orders of magnitude above the noise-free floor, so their errors are visible to the
data and are not hidden along the null direction; how they nevertheless reach such small projection errors is not
established by this profile.]{#clm-0040 .claim} The conclusion rests on that excess projection error and not on the size of the
compensating terms. Their calcification (0 to $1.8\times10^{-3}$ in tissue) and their deviation of the tissue sum from one (0.03 to 0.08) are
comparable to what steps along the null direction of the size of their adipose errors (steps of about 0.1 to 1) would
need (calcification 0.0008 to 0.008, sum change 0.003 to 0.03), so those two quantities alone would not exclude it. This sits alongside the previous chapter's finding that nearly all their
error scores as "along the null direction": that metric cannot distinguish an error the data hide from an error they can see,
because the null direction is almost a pure exchange.

A candidate explanation is spatial structure. In a Stage-0 calculation on 20 training cases, noise-free and around the true
solution, the true maps were perturbed by three synthetic exchange fields: a uniform one, a smooth random field (Gaussian
smoothed on a scale of 20 pixels, normalised to a peak magnitude of one) and a rough field (an independent random sign in
every pixel). The projection mean-squared error grew as $c\,t^2$ with $c=1.7\times10^{-4}$ (uniform), $4.5\times10^{-6}$
(smooth), $8.0\times10^{-7}$ (rough) and $1.6\times10^{-9}$ (exact null direction).
[Spatially varying exchange fields are far less visible to the projection loss than a uniform one: the fitted coefficients
imply amplitudes about 6 times (smooth field) and 14 times (rough field) smaller for the same residual (38 and 210 times in
mean-squared error), so a projection MSE of $10^{-6}$, about the level the physics-only networks reach, is compatible with
exchange steps up to 0.077 (uniform), 0.47 (smooth) and 1.1 (rough), and a residual of $2\times10^{-8}$, the projection error left
after physics refinement of the supervised network (whose material error stays at 0.0177), with steps up to 0.011, 0.067 and 0.16.]{#clm-0064 .claim}
Here a step of size $t$ is along the unit vector $(-1,+1,0)/\sqrt{2}$, so the change in each material's volume fraction is $t/\sqrt{2}$.
The fitted law is quadratic and was fitted close to the truth: steps of 0.47 and 1.1 extrapolate it well beyond the range
over which it was fitted and, for amplitudes near or above 1, beyond the physical range of 0 to 1 for a volume fraction, so
the larger figures are rough extrapolations.
A network error that varies rapidly across the image can therefore be both large and nearly invisible to a loss that is
averaged over rays. Two cautions apply. The synthetic fields are stand-ins; the records do not show that the networks' actual
errors have these spatial statistics. And the smooth field is normalised by its peak, so part of its apparent invisibility
reflects a smaller typical amplitude than the quoted step, which makes the comparison with the uniform field a statement about
peak amplitude. This is an analysis around the truth with synthetic fields on training cases and has not been reviewed.

## Which priors can discriminate?

A prior that treats adipose and fibroglandular tissue symmetrically cannot prefer the true spatial arrangement over its
exchanged version. Stage 0 evaluated four label-free priors and one prior that uses training labels: the absence of
calcification (an absolute-value penalty and a smoothed count of non-zero calcification), a bimodality penalty (the tissue
average of $a(1-a)$, with $a$ the adipose share of the tissue), the total variation of $a$ over tissue, and a match to the
distribution of $a$ measured on other training cases (a sliced Wasserstein distance).
[The calcification-absence, bimodality and total-variation priors are exactly invariant under relabelling adipose as
fibroglandular and vice versa (the change in the prior is zero to $10^{-17}$); of the priors analysed only the training-label
marginal discriminates, and it counts as weak supervision (this analysis is unreviewed and uses training cases around the
truth).]{#clm-0041 .claim} For the label-free priors, whatever margin the data give to the true labelling therefore comes
from the data term alone. This is consistent with the simple priors of the previous chapter doing nothing, but it does not by
itself explain the nearly uniform adipose values the physics-only networks produce. The entropy and range-hinge priors of the
previous chapter were not part of this analysis; the bimodality penalty here is a different, quadratic form.

On the pre-registered gate of that stage, the smoothed calcification count, the bimodality penalty and the train-marginal
prior passed, the absolute-value calcification penalty passed only at the residual level of the classical solver, and total
variation failed because its profile decreases along the null direction. The bimodal pass is partly by construction (the true
maps are close to pure tissue), and the weight windows used training labels, so the windows themselves are not label-free.
[The calcification and sum priors act on the null direction only and have no effect on exchange fields, and the trained
networks already satisfy them approximately; this weakens the idea that supplying calcification or sum knowledge would, by
itself, repair the dominant network failure, which is a spatially varying adipose error, while leaving the per-ray result
below untouched.]{#clm-0097 .claim} This is an interpretation of preliminary profiles. These priors are also blind to sign, and the earlier chapter reports that the baseline
networks' adipose maps are anticorrelated with the true map (@sec-labelfree), so a prior that rescued the split would have to fix
the tissue ordering and not only break the symmetry; this observation is from a different analysis and has not been tested against any prior.

## How much does acquisition matter?

A single-ray Cramér–Rao analysis compares single-energy, dual-energy and photon-counting acquisitions at equal incident
photons (not equal dose), with an ideal detector and no K-edge, over nine path-length and composition cases (path lengths of
2, 6 and 12 cm; adipose-rich, even and fibroglandular-rich mixtures, no calcification in the true composition); the
photon-counting case uses the 80 kVp beam only. The quantity bounded is the standard deviation of the adipose fraction along
the ray. In the "sum known" cases the total path length is taken as known.

| Condition | Dual-energy | Photon counting (32 bins) |
|---|---|---|
| Calcification unknown, sum known (6 cm, 50/50 case) | 0.249 | 0.120 |
| Calcification known absent, sum known | 0.024–0.042 | 0.026–0.046 |
| Calcification known absent, sum unknown (reviewer calculation, not bound to a run record) | about 0.20 | about 0.10 |

: Cramér–Rao standard deviation of the adipose fraction per ray (dimensionless), at $2\times10^5$ incident photons. Across the nine cases the first row ranges from 0.23 to 0.48 (dual-energy) and 0.12 to 0.22 (photon counting), a ratio of 1.9–2.2; the second row is the nine-case range. In the second row a single 50 kVp measurement alone gives 0.021–0.035 and a single 80 kVp measurement 0.029–0.053. The third row comes from an independent reviewer's calculation; the case and bin count were not recorded. With calcification also unknown and the sum unknown, dual-energy is not identifiable (rank 2 for three unknowns) and the photon-counting rank depends on a threshold.
{#tbl-crb}

[In a single-ray analysis (ideal detector, $2\times10^5$ incident photons, nine path-length and composition cases) with the
sum known and calcification unknown, adding spectral bins improves the adipose-fraction Cramér–Rao uncertainty by at most
about a factor of two (dual-energy 0.249 against 0.120 for 32 photon-counting bins in the 6 cm, 50/50 case; ratio 1.9–2.2
over all nine cases); with calcification known absent and the sum known, dual-energy already reaches 0.024–0.042 and photon
counting adds nothing (0.026–0.046), the best single measurement being the 50 kVp beam alone (0.021–0.035).]{#clm-0042 .claim}
[With calcification known absent but the sum unknown, a reviewer's calculation gave about 0.20 for dual-energy against about
0.10 for photon counting; this number is not bound to a run record and its case and bin count were not recorded.]{#clm-0098 .claim}
The first two rows are computed by the project's own script and reproduce exactly from that run's theory output, but the
evidence check for the finding reports no numeric bindings, so they are not bound to registered metrics in the strict sense;
the third is a reviewer's calculation and should be treated as an unverified cross-check. In the dual-energy design the
photons are split equally between the two tube voltages, whereas the photon-counting bins share a single 80 kVp beam of the same
total, so the comparison is at equal total photons. Reading across rows, the roughly tenfold gain comes from knowing calcification is absent
while the sum is known; with the sum unknown, bins again help by about a factor of two. [The dominant lever for resolving the
adipose/fibroglandular split is knowledge about calcification and the sum of the fractions, not additional spectral
bins.]{#clm-0043 .claim} This is an interpretation of a variance bound that ignores bias from model mismatch, without
tomographic coupling or spatial priors; the benchmark data are noiseless, so the photon number is a hypothetical noise level;
the bound refers to a ray, not a pixel; and the "known" rows were added after a reviewer pointed out they were missing. It
also says nothing about whether calcification is in fact absent: real cases contain calcified lesions.

## The staged test

The plan is staged so that information and optimisation are separated. Stage 0, the deterministic profiles above, has been
run. Stage 1 fits each case on its own, with an optimiser run to convergence, supplying the material information directly
instead of a network; if the adipose split is recovered there from an uninformative start, information is sufficient and
the earlier network failures were optimisation-limited; if it is not, the problem is conditioning-limited. Stage 2 would
then study network priors. [Converged per-case solves with oracle knowledge of the support are intended to test how much
information the priors carry once optimisation is removed; only if that passes a gate will network priors be
studied.]{#clm-0045 .claim}

### What the Stage 1 pilot did

The project owner approved a bounded pilot, with its decision rules registered before any pilot run. It used three
validation cases chosen only by their number of calcified pixels (lowest, 557; median, 1062; highest, 1441), for
representativeness and not tuned. [The pilot used noiseless data and a full-view (256 views, two tube voltages) L-BFGS
optimiser limited to 1000 iterations in single precision; in the arms that fix the tissue sum (A, B and D) the sum was
supplied by an oracle occupancy map taken from the truth, so these arms measure information limits when the sum is known,
not label-free recovery.]{#clm-0100 .claim} Arm A also forced calcification to zero, leaving one unknown per pixel (the
adipose share); arm B freed calcification with a sparsity penalty; arm D added the bimodality prior to arm A; arm C freed
all three fractions with no sum constraint; and a further arm (A_img) used a support derived from the images instead of the
oracle. Starting points were a uniform guess, an image-derived guess and, as oracle controls, the truth plus a 0.3-amplitude
uniform, smooth or random exchange pattern (or null-direction pattern). Each solve is deterministic and was run once, so
there are no seeds or replicates.

The error measure is the root-mean-square difference of the three material-fraction maps from the truth, in volume-fraction
units, after clipping the estimates to the physical range from 0 to 1. A *converged* solve was defined as a final
projection mean-squared error of at most $10^{-8}$, and a *recovered* one as a clipped error of at most 0.05 together with
an error of at most 0.05 in the adipose fraction at spatial frequencies above 1/8 cycle per pixel.

### What each arm showed

[In arm A, with calcification fixed at zero and the sum known, the solver reached a projection mean-squared error of
$1.7\times10^{-9}$ on the case with the fewest calcified pixels and $2.4\times10^{-8}$ and $3.2\times10^{-8}$ on the other
two; five different starting points ended at essentially the same solution on each case (one basin, which is not a proof of
uniqueness), and the clipped error, about 0.31 from a uniform start, fell to 0.014, 0.048 and 0.044 on the three
cases.]{#clm-0101 .claim} Only the first case met the convergence target; the other two stopped on a plateau above it.
[Without clipping the same error is 0.209, 0.355 and 0.435, so clipping removes 98 to 99.5% of the squared error and most of
the unclipped error comes from estimates outside the physical range.]{#clm-0102 .claim}

The high-frequency adipose error was reported as 0.21, 0.35 and 0.42 for arm A against the criterion of 0.05, and was first
read as "converged but not recovered". [That high-frequency metric was computed on the unclipped estimates, so it is
probably dominated by out-of-range excursions near calcifications and is not evidence that the spatially varying error was
left unrecovered; a clipped, away-from-lesion version has been coded but had not been run when the records were last
updated.]{#clm-0103 .claim} Whether a spatially varying adipose error remains once excursions and lesion neighbourhoods
are separated is therefore undecided.

[Arm A cannot represent calcified lesions: with the true adipose map and calcification forced to zero the projection error
cannot go below $1.0\times10^{-7}$, $2.0\times10^{-6}$ and $2.4\times10^{-6}$ on the three cases, so it is not a clean
positive control. On the lowest-count case the solver nevertheless reached $1.7\times10^{-9}$, below that floor, which is
possible only by bending the adipose map away from the truth near the lesions.]{#clm-0044 .claim} The pilot's own positive
control for this arm (oracle-perturbed starts converging to $10^{-8}$ and recovering) failed on all three cases, so under
the rules registered for the pilot the non-recoveries described next are control or solver failures until shown otherwise.

[With calcification free (arm B) and a uniform start, the solver had not converged at the iteration cap (projection error
$5$ to $6\times10^{-8}$, still falling by 11 to 13% per 200 iterations) and the remaining error was mostly low-frequency
(0.14, with a clipped error of 0.10 to 0.12); from the truth plus a random exchange pattern it stalled at $4\times10^{-8}$
with the clipped error unchanged at 0.14; from the truth plus a null-direction pattern it returned to within 0.011 to 0.015
of the truth at a projection error of 1.4 to $1.8\times10^{-8}$, short of the convergence target.]{#clm-0104 .claim}
[No starting point that was not given oracle information was shown to be both converged and recovered.]{#clm-0105 .claim}
[Nearly invisible perturbations persisted while visible ones were removed, the same ordering as in the Stage 0 visibility
results; this rests on two comparisons and compares magnitudes only, so it is not a quantitative test, and whether the
uniform-start case is limited by information or by the solver is not decided.]{#clm-0106 .claim}

[The bimodality prior (arm D, one weight of $10^{-5}$) gave no gain over arm A: the clipped error was 0.087 to 0.100 against
0.014 to 0.048, and the projection error ($3.4$ to $7.2\times10^{-8}$) had not converged.]{#clm-0107 .claim}

### What was not tested

[Arms C and A_img did not test sum-free identifiability: an image-derived support cannot hold partial-volume pixels, so the
oracle-perturbed starting points of arm C, once restricted to that support, already had a projection error of 1.6 to
$1.75\times10^{-5}$ against $1.8\times10^{-16}$ for the unrestricted truth; every start of arm C stopped at the iteration cap
at 2.7 to $2.8\times10^{-6}$ and was still falling by about 1.4% per 100 iterations, and arm A_img stopped at 4.7 to
$4.9\times10^{-6}$. Support misspecification is a plausible explanation but was inferred, not isolated, and a solver limit
is not excluded.]{#clm-0108 .claim} The band errors reported for these two arms are artefacts of the metric (a ratio
with a near-zero sum for arm C, unclipped excursions outside the mask for arm A_img) and are not quoted.

[The first submission of arm C crashed with non-finite values because the spectral tables carry energies of 1.25 to 3.25 keV
that have zero spectrum weight but very large attenuation coefficients (up to about $1.5\times10^{3}$ and $3.2\times10^{4}$
cm$^{-1}$ for fibroglandular tissue and calcification); for slightly negative fractions, produced by line-search steps in
the unbounded arm, the exponential overflowed to infinity and zero times infinity gave not-a-number. Dropping the
zero-weight energies, which is exact on finite paths, fixed it, and arms A and B were unaffected.]{#clm-0109 .claim}
Any other free-fraction solver on this forward model needs the same guard.

### Review status and what remains

[All four pilot findings are preliminary. The three about the converged arms, the free-calcification arms and the
sum-free and bimodality arms were each judged by an independent targeted review to need work, and their wording was
corrected afterwards; the fourth, on the numerical failure, was judged supported but stays preliminary because its numbers
are not bound to run records. No later review is recorded.]{#clm-0110 .claim}

[The pilot did not test the registered success rule (recovery on at least 18 of 20 validation cases), sum-free
identifiability, label-free recovery with an image-derived support, noise, or the test split; the clipped and away-from-lesion
rerun, a longer solve for the free-calcification arm from a uniform start, and a lesion-free or synthetic case that would
separate misspecification from non-identifiability had not been run, and whether to start the network-prior stage (Stage 2)
at all was left to the project owner; Stage 2 and the acquisition ablation are proposed and have not been
started.]{#clm-0111 .claim} The most recent project checkpoint records the pilot as complete and awaiting the owner's
review.

What can be said, provisionally, is narrow. With the tissue sum supplied and calcification removed, the solves reduced
the clipped map error to a few percent of the volume fraction in an arm that cannot represent calcified lesions, but only one of
the three cases met the convergence rule, the unclipped error remained 0.21 to 0.44, and the arm's own positive control failed,
so the pilot does not show that optimisation has ceased to be the limit even when the sum is known. Whether
the spatially varying adipose error is recoverable without oracle knowledge of the sum has not been tested, because the
arms designed to test it failed for modelling and numerical reasons. Until the pilot's open points are resolved and reviewed,
nothing in this chapter says that calcification or sum knowledge works in practice.
